en: The Upadeśa on the Lotus Sutra, Part 1:
The Introduction Chapter,
composed by Vasubandhu Bodhisattva.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati from Central India, together with Senglang and others, during the Northern Wei Dynasty. Thus have I heard:

At one time the Buddha was dwelling on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha, accompanied by a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus. All were arhats whose outflows were exhausted and who were no longer subject to afflictions; they had attained mastery over their minds, having well attained liberation of mind and well attained liberation through wisdom. Their minds were thoroughly disciplined; they were great dragons among men, having done what was to be done and accomplished their task. They had laid down all heavy burdens, achieved their own benefit, and exhausted the fetters of existence. Having well attained right knowledge, they were entirely liberated in mind; they had attained mastery over their minds and reached the foremost shore.

There were eighty thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all of whom were non-retrogressive regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*; they had all attained *dhāraṇīs* and great eloquence in joyful exposition, and turned the wheel of Dharma that never regresses. They had made offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of buddhas and planted roots of goodness in the presence of those buddhas. They were constantly praised by all the buddhas; they cultivated their bodies and minds through great compassion, skillfully entered the Buddha’s wisdom, and attained mastery over great knowledge to reach the other shore. Their fame was heard throughout immeasurable worlds, and they were able to deliver countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings.
In this Dharma-gate, the first chapter elucidates the accomplishment of seven kinds of merit.
What are these seven?
First is the accomplishment of the introduction (*nidāna*).
Second, the accomplishment of the assembly;
third, the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s arrival at the time to preach the Dharma;
fourth, the accomplishment of abiding in accordance with the dignified deportment required for the basis of preaching the Dharma.
Fifth is the accomplishment of the basis for teaching the causes;
sixth is the accomplishment of the great assembly being present and desiring to hear the Dharma;
seventh is the accomplishment of Mañjuśrī’s response.
Furthermore, regarding the accomplishment of the introductory section, this Dharma-gate manifests the accomplishment of two kinds of meanings. What are these two?
First, it manifests the supreme accomplishment among all Dharma-gates.
Second, it is because of the manifestation of the accomplishment of sovereign merit;
for example, the city of Rājagṛha surpasses all other cities and dwellings, and Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa surpasses all other mountains.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "Thus have I heard:
at one time the Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain in the city of Rājagṛha.
Regarding the accomplishment of the assembly, there are four kinds of accomplishments.
What are the four?
First, accomplishment in number;
second, accomplishment in practice.
Third is the accomplishment of the gathering of merits;
fourth is the accomplishment of abiding in majestic deportment according to the Dharma.
As for the accomplishment of number, it refers to the fact that the great assembly is incalculable.
There are four types of those who accomplish practice:
first, all śrāvakas who cultivate the practices of the Hīnayāna;
second, all bodhisattvas who cultivate the practices of the Mahāyāna.

Third, because various bodhisattvas manifest at appropriate times as being able to practice the Mahāyāna—such as the sixteen individuals including Bhadrapāla—who, while fully possessing the inconceivable deeds of a bodhisattva, can manifest in various forms such as upāsakas, upāsikās, bhikṣus, and bhikṣuṇīs;
fourth, because the deportment of those who have left the household life is fixed and uniform, which differs from that of bodhisattvas.
The sixteen phrases beginning with "All are arhats" demonstrate the accomplishment of the merits of the śrāvakas.
The thirteen phrases beginning with "All are non-retrogressive regarding anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" demonstrate the accomplishment of the merits of the bodhisattvas.
Regarding the accomplishment of the virtues of an Arhat, it should be understood that those sixteen phrases demonstrate the meaning as subsumed under three types of gates.
What are these three gates?
First, the gate of progressive superiority; [and so forth].
Second is the gate of general and specific characteristics;
third is the gate of encompassing matters.

Regarding the gate of successive arising: because all outflows (*āsrava*) have been exhausted, one is called an Arhat; because the mind has attained mastery, the outflows are said to be exhausted; and because the outflows are exhausted, one is named an Arhat.

Because the mind is free from afflictions, it is said that the mind has attained mastery; because one has well attained liberation of mind and well attained liberation through wisdom, it is said that the mind has attained mastery.
Because one is far removed from both the seer and the seen, it is called "no further afflictions.
Because one has already well attained liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, it is called "the mind is well-tamed."
The Great Dragon among Men traverses all evil paths as if they were level roads, unimpeded by anything.
This is because he has already performed what was to be done and has already reached the destination that was to be reached.
"What ought to be done has been done" means that these great dragons among men have exhausted all that is to be countered, having subdued the enemies that are the afflictions (*kleśa*).
"What was to be accomplished has been accomplished" means that they will not be reborn hereafter, as their tasks corresponding to their respective stages have already been completed.
"Having laid down all heavy burdens" means that one has done what was to be done and completed what was to be accomplished, because the heavy burden of future rebirth has already been cast off.
"Having attained one's own benefit" means that one has cast off the burden and realized *nirvāṇa*.
"One who has exhausted all fetters of existence" refers to one who has already attained their own benefit, because they have severed the causes of all afflictions.
"One who has well-attained right knowledge and liberation of mind" refers to one for whom all outflows (*āsrava*) have been extinguished.
Those who have attained mastery over all minds do so because they skillfully know and see the wisdom of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.

Those who have reached the supreme further shore do so because they have skillfully attained right knowledge and liberation of mind, and have skillfully acquired various meritorious qualities such as the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and the concentration of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*).
Regarding the "Great Arhats" and so forth: they have attained mastery over their minds and reached the other shore.
Regarding those "known by all": they are recognized by kings, princes, ministers, Śakra, Brahmā, and others.
Furthermore, because Śrāvakas, Bodhisattvas, Buddhas, and others possess supreme wisdom, and because those with supreme wisdom are all well-known, they are called "those known by many.
Regarding the general and specific categories, all sixteen phrases beginning with "Arhat" constitute this section; the first phrase is general, while the remaining phrases are specific.
Regarding the phrase "all are arhats," one should know that the name "arhat" possesses fifteen meanings:
first, because they are worthy of receiving offerings and respect such as food, drink, bedding, and requisites;
second, because they are worthy of leading the great assembly to transform and teach all beings.
Third, because one should enter villages, cities, and so forth;
fourth, because one should subdue various non-Buddhists and others;
fifth, because one should swiftly examine phenomena with wisdom.
Sixth, one should preach the Dharma neither too hastily nor too slowly, remaining tireless so as to accord with the Dharma;
seventh, one should sit in quietude in secluded places, neither hoarding nor accumulating food, clothing, or any necessities of life, because of having few desires and knowing contentment;
eighth, one should practice exclusively wholesome deeds without becoming attached to the various dhyānas.
Ninth, because one should practice the noble conduct of emptiness;
tenth, because one should practice the noble conduct of signlessness;
eleventh, because one should practice the noble conduct of wishlessness.
Twelfth, because one should subdue the mundane mind through the purity of dhyāna;
thirteenth, because one should give rise to the supreme merit of the various supernormal powers (abhijñā);
fourteenth, because one should realize the merit of the ultimate truth (paramārtha).
Fifteenth, one should know as it truly is that the assembly born together attains all merits for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings.
Regarding the "gate of the inclusion of matters," these fifteen phrases include ten kinds of merit, demonstrating both the expressible fruit and the inexpressible fruit.
First, there is the manifestation of two phrases that encompass the attainment of merit, as the sūtra says: “All outflows are exhausted, and there are no further afflictions.
Second, there are three phrases that encompass all merits, and one phrase for the merit of subduing the world, as the sūtra says: “The mind has attained mastery”;
and two phrases for the merit of subduing those in training who transcend the world, as the sūtra says: “Well-attained liberation of mind, well-attained liberation through wisdom.”
Third is the inclusion of the merit of non-contradiction, because one accords with the practice of the Tathāgata’s teachings, as the sūtra says, "the mind is well-tamed.
Fourth is the inclusion of superior merit, as the sūtra says, "a great dragon among men."
Fifth is the inclusion of the supreme merit that ought to be performed.

That which ought to be performed consists in making offerings to, honoring, respecting, and revering the Tathāgata in accordance with the Dharma; as the sūtra says, "one performs what ought to be performed."
Sixth is the inclusion of the perfection of merit, because the stage of training is fulfilled, as the sūtra says, "What was to be done has been accomplished.
Seventh is the inclusion of the merit of transcending through three phrases:
first, transcending reception; [and so forth].
Second, because they have transcended seeking life-sustenance, offerings, and honor;
third, because they have transcended the lower and upper realms and have passed beyond the stages of training (*śaikṣabhūmi*).
As the Sūtra says: "They have laid down all heavy burdens, attained their own benefit, and exhausted the fetters of existence (*bhavasaṃyojana*)."
Eighth is the inclusion of the supreme and unsurpassed merit, as the sūtra says: "having well attained right knowledge and liberation of mind.
Ninth is the inclusion of the merit of performing what is beneficial for sentient beings, as the sūtra says: "attaining mastery over all minds."
Tenth is the merit of encompassing the foremost [qualities], as stated in the sutra: "reaching the first shore.
It should be understood that those thirteen phrases of merit for the bodhisattvas are subsumed under two categories:
first, the category of the upper and lower branches; and second, the category of the primary and secondary factors.
Second is the gate of the inclusion of matters.
Regarding the gate of the upper and lower branches, it should be understood that these consist of the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and the specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*).
The phrase "all [of them] do not regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*" is the general characteristic; the remainder are the specific characteristics.
There are ten manifestations of that non-retrogression:
first, abiding in non-retrogression through hearing the Dharma, as the sutra says, "because they have all attained dhāraṇīs."
Second is the non-retrogression of eloquence, as the sutra says, "great eloquence and delight in teaching.
Third is the non-retrogression of teaching, as the sutra says, "turning the irreversible wheel of Dharma."

Fourth is non-retrogression by relying on spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), because one relies on the physical body (*rūpakāya*) through the activities of body and mind; as the sūtra says: "making offerings to immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas" and "planting various roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) in the presence of those Buddhas."
Fifth is the non-retrogression of severing all doubts, as the sutra states: "They are constantly praised by all Buddhas.

Sixth is the non-retrogression of entering into each respective teaching according to whatever matters one expounds for others, as the sutra states: "One cultivates body and mind through great compassion."
Seventh is the non-retrogression from entering the realm of omniscience as it truly is, as stated in the sutra: "skillfully entering the Buddha’s wisdom.
Eighth is the non-retrogression based on the emptiness of self and the emptiness of phenomena, as stated in the sutra: "penetrating great wisdom."
Ninth is non-retrogression in entering the realm of reality as it is, as the sūtra says, "reaching the other shore.
Tenth is non-retrogression in abiding by what ought to be done, as the sūtra says, "being able to deliver immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings."

Regarding the "gate of grasping the subject matter," this demonstrates in which purified stages the bodhisattvas abide, by what means, and within what spheres of experience they should perform their respective duties.
Regarding "purity of the ground," it refers to the purity and tranquility of signless practice (*animitta-caryā*) in the three stages from the eighth stage upward.
There are four kinds of skillful means (*upāya*):
first, the skillful means of grasping the sublime Dharma and maintaining the sublime Dharma, because one preaches it for others through the power of eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Second is the skillful means of embracing spiritual friends, because one performs what ought to be done by relying upon spiritual friends;
third is the skillful means of embracing sentient beings, because one does not abandon sentient beings;
fourth is the skillful means of embracing wisdom, because one teaches and transforms sentient beings so that they may enter into that wisdom.
The "spheres" (*viṣaya*) are easy to understand.

Furthermore, there is the "gate of the objects of appropriation," which demonstrates that the superior qualities appropriated in the various stages (*bhūmi*) differ from the qualities of the two vehicles (*yāna*).
Regarding the eighth stage: it is because non-effortful wisdom (*anābhoga-jñāna*) differs from both the lower and the upper stages.
It does not resemble the lower because the effortful practices of the lower stages cannot move it;
it does not resemble the upper because the signless practices of the upper stages cannot move it, as it proceeds spontaneously.
Within the ninth stage, one attains the *dhāraṇī* gate of superior progress because of being fully endowed with the four types of unimpeded mastery.

Within the tenth stage, one attains the irreversible wheel of Dharma and receives the empowerment of a Buddha, just like the son of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), because of having attained the merit of identical inclusion.
Regarding the accomplishment of the gathering of merit, it is demonstrated by way of what basis, what mind, what wisdom, what objective sphere of activity, and what capacity for accomplishment.
As for what it relies upon: it relies upon spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
As for what kind of mind it relies upon: it relies upon the minds of sentient beings, teaching and transforming them in order to ultimately benefit all sentient beings.
Regarding "by what wisdom": it relies on three kinds of wisdom:
first, the secret wisdom of bestowing predictions;
second, the wisdom of the various supernormal powers; [and third, the wisdom of the ultimate fruit].
Third is true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*).
One should understand that it is comprised of three types of knowledge: that which acts in dependence upon a particular object, and that which acts in dependence upon a particular agent.
Regarding the accomplishment of abiding in conduct according to the Dharma, there are four modes of manifestation.
What are the four?
First, being surrounded by the fourfold assembly;
second, [being preceded and followed] by them before and behind;
Third is making offerings and showing respect;
fourth is honoring and praising.
This is as stated in the sutra: "At that time, the World-Honored One was surrounded by the fourfold assembly, who made offerings to him, showed him respect, honored him, and praised him."
Regarding "when the Tathāgata wishes to preach the Dharma, it reaches fulfillment": this is because he preaches Mahāyāna sūtras for the sake of all bodhisattvas.
One should know that this Mahāyāna sūtra has seventeen names which reveal its profound merits.
It is called the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* because it accomplishes the meaning of its words; for by means of this Dharma-gate, it expounds that most profound and wondrous realm of reality.
This most profound and wondrous realm is the supreme realm of all Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
Second, it is called the "Most Excellent Sūtra" because it accomplishes the most wondrous and supreme treasury among the Three Baskets (Tripiṭaka).
Third, it is called "Mahāvaipulya" because it accomplishes the maintenance of immeasurable Mahāyāna gateways according to the faculties of sentient beings.
The fourth is called "the Dharma for teaching Bodhisattvas," because it brings about the accomplishment of the Dharma according to the capacity of Bodhisattvas whose faculties have matured.
The fifth is called "that which is protected by the Buddhas' mindfulness," because this Dharma exists by virtue of the Buddha-Tathāgatas.
Sixth, it is called "The Secret Dharma of All Buddhas," because this dharma is so profound that only a Tathāgata knows it.
Seventh, it is called "The Treasury of All Buddhas," because the treasury of the Tathāgata’s merits and samādhis is contained within this sutra.
The eighth is named "The Secret Place of All Buddhas," because it is not granted to sentient beings whose faculties are not yet matured, as they are not vessels for the Dharma.
The ninth is named "Able to Give Birth to All Buddhas," because upon hearing this Dharma-gate, one is able to attain the Bodhi of a Buddha.

The tenth is called "the site of enlightenment for all Buddhas," because by hearing this Dharma-gate one can achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, whereas this cannot be accomplished through other sūtras.
Eleventh, it is named "The Wheel of Dharma Turned by All Buddhas," because this dharma-gate can destroy all obstacles.
Twelfth, it is named "The Solid Relics of All Buddhas," meaning that the Tathāgata’s true suchness-dharmakāya is indestructible within this sūtra.

The thirteenth is titled *The Sūtra on the Great Skillful Means of All Buddhas*, because by relying on this dharma-gate, one realizes great bodhi and has already taught the dharmas for devas, humans, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and others for the sake of sentient beings.
The fourteenth is called "the Sūtra that Expounds the One Vehicle," for this Dharma-gate reveals the ultimate essence of the Tathāgata’s anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; the two vehicles are not ultimate.
Fifteenth, it is named "Abiding in the Ultimate Meaning" (paramārtha-vihāra), because this dharma-gate is the ultimate dwelling place of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
Sixteenth, it is named "The Lotus of the Sublime Dharma" (saddharma-puṇḍarīka); herein there are two meanings.
What are these two meanings?
First is the meaning of "emerging from water," because it signifies the inexhaustible transcendence of the turbid waters of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

Furthermore, there is another meaning: the lotus emerging from mud and water serves as a metaphor for the various *śrāvakas* entering and sitting within the great assembly of the Tathāgata; just as the various *bodhisattvas* sit upon lotuses, they hear the exposition of the pure realm of unsurpassed wisdom and realize the secret treasury of the Tathāgata.

Regarding the second, "the blossoming of flowers": because the assembly is timid and weak in heart regarding the Mahāyāna and thus unable to give rise to faith, [the Buddha] reveals the Tathāgata’s pure and wondrous Dharma-body so that they may develop faith.
The seventeenth is called the "Dharma-gate" because it encompasses accomplishment.
To encompass accomplishment means to include immeasurable bodies of names, phrases, and syllables, as well as verses such as the *piṇḍa* and *acchobha*.
These seventeen phrases constitute the general [teaching], while the remaining phrases are the specific ones;
as it says in the sutra: "For the sake of all bodhisattvas, he preached a Mahāyāna sūtra titled 'The Immeasurable Meanings,'" and so forth.
Regarding the accomplishment of abiding in accordance with the majestic deportment while teaching the Dharma based on its foundation: this demonstrates by what kind of dharmas one teaches the Dharma.
It is based on three kinds of dharmas:
first, because of the accomplishment of samādhi; for the accomplishment of samādhi, two kinds of manifestations are shown.
What are these two?
First, the accomplishment of sovereign power, because body and mind are immovable;
second, the departure from all obstacles, because one accords with sovereign power.
This sovereign power is of two kinds:
first, to accord with sentient beings by manifesting the remedial means for their gathering and awakening to the factors conducive to enlightenment;

second, to counteract the deeply entrenched afflictions accumulated over immeasurable lifetimes, as stated in the sutra: "Having spoken this sutra, he sat cross-legged and entered the Samādhi of the Station of Immeasurable Meaning," and so forth.

Second, based on the receptacle world; third, based on the world of sentient beings—because it causes the world to tremble and because it knows the events of immeasurable kalpas in the past, and so forth.

As it is said in the sutra: "At that time, the heavens rained down *māndārava* flowers, and so on, until [the assembly], filled with joy, joined their palms and gazed upon the Buddha with a single mind.

Regarding the accomplishment of the cause for teaching based on reliance: when that great assembly perceives extraordinary signs and inconceivable events, they think, "The Tathāgata should speak for my sake," and out of thirsting longing and the desire to hear, they give rise to a sense of rare wonder; this is called the accomplishment of the cause for teaching based on reliance.
Therefore, he emits great rays of light to manifest various events within all worlds.
First, he manifests external phenomena such as the sixfold earthquake; subsequently, he manifests the profound and secret Dharma realized within this Dharma-gate.

Furthermore, based on the world of the vessel (*bhājana-loka*) and the world of sentient beings (*sattva-loka*), [the Buddha] manifests the Three Jewels by way of their various numbers and various measures, as well as their distinctions in terms of the possession of afflictions and the possession of purification, and the distinctions between the Buddha-dharma and its disciples.

Furthermore, regarding the distinctions of vehicles, there are worlds where a Buddha exists and worlds where no Buddha exists; this causes sentient beings to see those who practice as not yet having attained the fruit, and those who have attained the Way as having already attained the fruit.
This is because the sutras speak of those who "practice and attain the Way.
Regarding the various types [of practitioners], this demonstrates the various modes of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
Briefly stated, there are four kinds of contemplation:
First, food;
second, hearing the Dharma;
third, clear practice.
The fourth is joy (*sukha*).

As the sutra states: "At that time, the Buddha emitted a light from the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows, up until the point where stupas made of the seven precious gems were erected for the Buddha's relics."

One who practices the bodhisattva path should understand that they transform sentient beings by employing the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) as skillful means for their gathering; this should be inferred from what is taught in the sūtras.

From this point onward, it is shown that the great assembly, desiring to hear the Dharma in their presence, has achieved its purpose. Although the Buddha questions only one person, the desire to hear arises in many who develop a sense of wonder; therefore, he questions Mañjuśrī alone, thus demonstrating that the World-Honored One’s disciples comply with the Dharma without contradiction.
Now, for what purpose does the Buddha, the World-Honored One, manifest this sign of supernatural transformation?
It is for the sake of manifesting the causes of the Great Signs.

As for these Great Signs, they are manifested as auspicious omens to proclaim the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, specifically to proclaim such phrases as "the wondrous Dharma that has been attained" and "inconceivable."
There are two reasons why Mañjuśrī is praised:
first, because he perceives all phenomena directly;
second, because he accomplishes those phenomena through his own mind, free from all causes and conditions.

Regarding the manifestation of various auspicious signs, it should be understood that each respective phenomenon is manifested, appears, disappears, abides, and ceases according to its nature; this is because Mañjuśrī is able to prophesy those phenomena, and because the causes and conditions for Mañjuśrī’s activities are accomplished, such that those dharmas are directly perceived.
The accomplishment of what is to be done is of two kinds:
first, the accomplishment of merit;
second, the accomplishment of wisdom.
The accomplishment of the cause is the accomplishment of all-knowledge.
The causal condition is the mark.
The fruit is the preaching of the Great Dharma.
Regarding "various Buddha-lands," it should be understood that this demonstrates the various distinctions within those lands.
A "pure and wondrous land" is so called because it is the dwelling place of sentient beings free from afflictions.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "It illuminates eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, even to the point that all the adornments of those Buddha-lands are seen.
The Tathāgata is the leader because all the bodhisattvas and others dwell in reliance upon the Tathāgata, and because the Tathāgata has attained mastery among all the great assemblies in those lands.
As it says in the sutra, "Furthermore, he sees the Buddhas currently residing in those lands," and so forth.

From this point onward, it clarifies how the noble Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, by means of his knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), directly perceives the characteristics of causes and effects from the past; having accomplished ten kinds of matters as if they were present before him, he is thus able to answer Maitreya.
Regarding the manifestation of the characteristics of past causes: it is because Mañjuśrī himself sees his own body practicing various deeds within those buddha-fields.

Regarding the manifestation of the characteristics of past results: it is because Mañjuśrī himself sees that he was the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light in the past, who heard this Dharma-gate from that Buddha and preached it for the sake of sentient beings.
Regarding the accomplishment of ten matters, what are these ten?
First, the accomplishment of the cause for manifesting the great purpose;
second, the accomplishment of the cause for manifesting the profound meaning of worldly letters, phrases, and sentences.
Third, the accomplishment of the cause for manifesting rare wonders;
fourth, the accomplishment of the cause for manifesting supreme excellence;
fifth, the accomplishment of the cause for manifesting great enjoyment.
Sixth, the accomplishment of the cause for manifestly perceiving the appropriation of the wheel of Dharma of all Buddhas;
seventh, the accomplishment of the cause for manifestly perceiving the well-firm and solid wheel of Dharma of the Tathāgata;
eighth, the accomplishment of the cause for manifestly perceiving the ability to enter [the path].
Ninth, the accomplishment of the cause consisting in direct perception and recollection;
tenth, the accomplishment of the cause consisting in direct perception of the events experienced by oneself.
Regarding the accomplishment of the cause of the great purpose, it should be understood that it is manifested through eight phrases:
First, they desire to turn the great wheel of Dharma;
second, they desire to rain down the great rain of Dharma;
third, they desire to beat the great drum of Dharma.
Fourth, they desire to erect the great banner of the Dharma;
fifth, they desire to light the great lamp of the Dharma;
sixth, they desire to blow the great conch of the Dharma.
Seventh, the desire not to cease the great Dharma drum;
eighth, the desire to expound the Great Dharma.
These eight phrases demonstrate that the Tathāgata intends to expound the Great Dharma and so forth.
What are the eight kinds of great meanings? They are:
for those who have doubts, to sever those doubts; for those whose doubts have already been severed, to increase and mature their wisdom-body;
and for those whose faculties are matured, to explain two kinds of secret realms, namely, the secret realm of the śrāvakas and the secret realm of the bodhisattvas.
The two phrases concerning the Great Dharma Drum manifest that [the teaching] is heard from afar.
"Entering the secret realm" means causing one to advance toward and attain the supreme, most pure meaning.
"Attaining the supreme, most pure meaning" means advancing toward and attaining the direct manifestation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*).
One who directly perceives all-knowledge does so for the sake of establishing names, phrases, and meanings for all phenomena.

Establishing names, phrases, and meanings is for the purpose of causing others to enter the turning of the wheel of Dharma through the ineffable realized wisdom, as it accomplishes the profound causal basis for the names, phrases, and meanings perceived in the world.
As it says in the Sūtra: "I have previously seen this omen under past Buddhas," up to, "therefore he manifests this omen.
This refers to the accomplishment of the cause for manifesting what is rare, because such a time cannot be found throughout immeasurable eons.
That which is inconceivable, incomparable, and immeasurable is demonstrated because it cannot be found even beyond those incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.
Furthermore, five kinds of kalpas are demonstrated:
first, the night; [and so forth].
Second, the day;
third, the month;
fourth, the season.
Fifth is the age (*kalpa*), which demonstrates those immeasurable and boundless eons. As the sutra states:

"In the past, immeasurable, boundless, inconceivable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons ago, there was a Buddha named Candrasūryapradīpa, who, up until his attainment of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, perfected all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
The manifestation of the accomplishment of supreme and wondrous causes is due to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifesting their own enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*).
As the Sūtra states: "Next, there was another Buddha also named Candrasūryapradīpa, up to and including the fact that the Dharma he taught was excellent in the beginning, middle, and end."

As for the accomplishment of the great cause of manifest enjoyment: at that time, the princes, having experienced supreme and wondrous bliss, each renounced their homes to become monks; furthermore, because that great assembly did not give rise to a mind of weariness throughout such a long duration.
As it is said in the Sūtra: "When that final Buddha had not yet left the household life, and even after he had bestowed the prophecy, he entered *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* at midnight."
The manifestation and perception of the accomplishment of the causes for all Buddhas to turn the wheel of Dharma is due to the non-interruption of the wheel of Dharma.
As the sūtra states: "After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva Wonderful Light upheld the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and expounded it for others for a full eighty minor kalpas."
The manifestation of the Tathāgata’s wheel of Dharma as being accomplished through its causes is because the Dharma was taught for immeasurable time after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.

The "profound" is the general [characteristic], while the others are the specific [characteristics].

Second is the profundity of substantial reality;

It is "wisdom" because it refers to the meaning of the knowledge of all aspects (sarvākārajñatā) and the wisdom of omniscience (sarvajñajñāna).

As it is said in the Sūtra: "The wisdom of all Buddhas is exceedingly profound and immeasurable; the gateway to that wisdom is difficult to see, difficult to awaken to, difficult to know, difficult to understand, and difficult to enter, such that it cannot be known by any Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."
The "gate of wisdom" refers to the teaching of the Āgamas.

"Śāriputra, the Dharma that is difficult to understand is what the Tathāgata is able to know.

Seventh is the entry into profundity; "entry into profundity" means that the meaning of the names, phrases, and sentences is difficult to grasp. As the sutra states: "Śāriputra!
The dharma that is difficult to understand is that which the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have taught according to what is appropriate; its underlying intent is difficult to comprehend.

Having thus explained the merits of the sublime Dharma, one should next understand the accomplishment of the Tathāgata’s merit as a Dharma-preacher.
As the Sūtra says: "For what reason?
Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have accomplished the causes for teaching with mastery."
Because the Tathāgata has accomplished four kinds of merit, he is able to deliver sentient beings.
What are these four?
The first is the accomplishment of abiding, as the sūtra says: "The Tathāgata accomplishes various skillful means."
"Various skillful means" refers to [the Buddha's career] from descending from Tuṣita Heaven until manifesting entry into nirvāṇa.
Second is "teaching and bringing to fulfillment," as indicated in the sūtra by the phrase "various knowledges and views."
"Various knowledges and views" refers to the manifestation of the various causes of defilement and purity.
Third is the ultimate accomplishment of merit, as stated in the sutra: "various mindfulnesses and contemplations."
"Various recollections and contemplations" refers to explaining the causes and conditions for accomplishing those dharmas in accordance with the Dharma.
Fourth is "explaining accomplishment," as in the sutra's phrase "various modes of expression."

Regarding "various modes of expression": by means of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), one relies upon various names, phrases, and syllables to teach according to what each respective sentient being is able to receive.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation:
"various skillful means" refers to manifesting the various kinds of faults of the heterodox teachings of non-Buddhists in such and such ways,
and manifesting the various kinds of merits of the Buddhas' true Dharma in such and such ways.

As it is said in the sutra: "Since my attainment of Buddhahood, I have extensively expounded the verbal teachings and used innumerable skillful means to guide sentient beings from their various attachments, enabling them to attain liberation."
Furthermore, "innumerable skillful means" refers to employing skillful means to cause entry into all wholesome dharmas.
Furthermore, "skillful means" refers to severing all doubts.
Furthermore, "skillful means" refers to causing entry into superior and supreme wisdom.
Furthermore, regarding skillful means: it is by relying on the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) that sentient beings are gathered and led to liberation.
As for those who are attached, they are attached here and there—whether attached to the realms (*dhātu*), or to the stages (*bhūmi*), or to the divisions (*aṅga*), or to the vehicles (*yāna*).
"Attachment to realms" refers to attachment to the realms of desire, form, and formlessness.

"Attachment to stages" refers to attachment to the stages of the meditative absorption of the first dhyāna through the stage of the neither-perception-nor-non-perception concentration and the stage of the cessation concentration, all of which involve the grasping of precepts and views.
"Attachment to categories" refers to attachment to the categories of the laity and the renunciants.
Attachment to the category of the laity refers to becoming attached to performing various actions, such as wrong views, together with those of one's own kind.
"Attachment to the category of renunciation" refers to attachment to fame, gain, various discursive thoughts, afflictions, and so forth.
"Attachment to vehicles" refers to attachment to the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Bodhisattva vehicle.
Those who adhere to the Śrāvaka vehicle delight in upholding the precepts of the Hīnayāna, seeking the fruits of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, and so forth.
Those who are attached to the Mahāyāna are attached to gain, offerings, and honor, as well as to the conceptual observation of the various characteristics of phenomena up to the stage of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, those with various types of knowledge and vision are those who have personally accomplished inconceivable realms, both for themselves and for śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge, vision, and skillful means have reached the other shore.
To have reached the other shore means that he surpasses all other bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, regarding the various modes of mindfulness and contemplation, it is as the Sūtra says:

"Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision are vast, profound, far-reaching, unobstructed, and unhindered; he is fully endowed with the powers, the fearlessnesses, the unique qualities, the faculties, the strengths, the factors of enlightenment, the meditative concentrations, the liberations, the samādhis, and the samāpattis."
Furthermore, the first accomplishment is for the sake of transforming sentient beings who are ready to be taught, by virtue of relying on spiritual friends for their accomplishment.
The second accomplishment is for the sake of enabling those whose faculties have matured to attain liberation.
The third is the family of the power of accomplishment (*siddhibala*), because it attains mastery, purity, and subjugation.
Fourth, it is taught that there are seven kinds of accomplishment (*siddhi*):
first, various accomplishments (*nānāsiddhi*), as the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra!..."
Because "the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have entered deeply into the boundless and have accomplished all unprecedented dharmas.

Second, regarding the term "accomplishment," it refers to attaining five kinds of exquisite vocal qualities when preaching the Dharma, as the sūtra states: "The Tathāgata is able to skillfully analyze and preach all dharmas in various ways; his words are gentle and pleasing to the hearts of the multitude."
Third is the accomplishment of the characteristics, as stated in the sūtra: "Cease, Śāriputra!
There is no need to speak further," because the minds of those sentient beings who are vessels for the Dharma have already been satisfied.

"Only Buddhas and Buddhas preach the Dharma, for the Tathāgatas alone are able to know the ultimate reality-mark (dharmatā) of that Dharma.

"Only the Buddha-Tathāgata knows all dharmas.

Seventh is the accomplishment of teaching the methods of practice in accordance with the inclinations of sentient beings. As for what those dharmas are and so forth, it is as the Sūtra says: "Śāriputra!..."
"Only the Buddha-Tathāgata can expound all dharmas. [This is because:

first, to gather in sentient beings through various gateways of the Dharma; second, to cause them to abide without distraction; third, to cause them to take up [the practice]; fourth, to cause them to attain liberation; fifth, to cause them to achieve the cultivation of the remedial dharmas (*pratipakṣa*); sixth, to enable the advancement and fulfillment of their cultivation; and seventh, to ensure that their cultivation is not lost.
These seven kinds of dharmas are for the sake of accomplishing what is to be done by all sentient beings and by oneself;
furthermore, they are for the accomplishment of teaching and transforming others, based upon the realization of the Dharma.
Furthermore, regarding the statement on "accomplishment," it refers to the basis of teaching the Dharma.
These two kinds of Dharma have been explained as previously stated.
Based upon these two kinds of Dharma, what is the sequence by which one attains practice?
It should be understood that those preceding phrases are repeated here.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of realization regarding the Dharma:
first, what is the Dharma?
Second, what is the dharma;
third, what is the dharma like;
fourth, what are the characteristics of the dharma.
Fifth, regarding the essence of the dharmas:
what are these dharmas? They are the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, and the dharmas of the Buddhas.
What is meant by "dharmas"? It refers to the teaching that gives rise to various matters.
As for what constitutes the nature of the Dharma, it is because one attains purity by means of three gates.
As for what constitutes the characteristic of the Dharma, it is because the three types of meanings share a single characteristic.
As for what constitutes the essence of the Dharma, it is because there is no duality of essence.
Regarding "non-dual essence": it means that although there are immeasurable vehicles, they are in fact only the single Buddha-vehicle, because there are no two vehicles.
Furthermore, there is another meaning:
as for "what kind of dharmas," this refers to conditioned dharmas and unconditioned dharmas.
What is meant by "dharmas"? It refers to conditioned dharmas (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*), unconditioned dharmas (*apratītyasamutpanna-dharma*), and so forth.
What is meant by "resembling dharmas"? It refers to permanent dharmas (*nitya-dharma*), impermanent dharmas (*anitya-dharma*), and the like.
Regarding the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmas*): they are the three characteristics of arising and so forth, and the three characteristics of non-arising and so forth.
Regarding the substance of phenomena: they are the substance of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the substance that is not the five aggregates.
Furthermore, what kind of phenomena are they? They are impermanent phenomena, conditioned phenomena, and phenomena produced by causes and conditions.
Furthermore, what characteristics do these phenomena have? They are phenomena characterized by visible marks and so forth.

Furthermore, as for the essence of phenomena (*dharmas*), it refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the grasper and the grasped; because the five aggregates constitute the collective essence of suffering, the five aggregates are also the essence of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*).
Furthermore, there is the teaching based on the Dharma:
what is the Dharma? It refers to the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables.
How is it the Dharma? Because it is that which has been taught by the Tathāgata.
What is the nature of the Dharma? It is that which is able to transform and teach sentient beings who are capable of being transformed.
What are the characteristics of the Dharma? They are grasped by means of sound, because those dharmas are grasped by relying upon sound.
Regarding "the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*): it is because the characteristics of phenomena are designated by way of conventional names.
From this point onward, it is demonstrated based on three meanings: first, the meaning of certainty;
[second, the meaning of non-contradiction; third, the meaning of non-duality].
